[Favorites 48](https://www.instagram.com/p/DfcfaLaAthr/) [Comments 1](https://www.instagram.com/p/DfcfaLaAthr/)

8 days ago

Where does one body end and another begin? 

In "Examinationscape" (2021), #JennaGribbon paints herself and her wife in overlapping passages that make their bodies difficult to untangle. A pointing gesture seems to promise clarity, but the brushwork keeps the boundaries between them unresolved. Even the marks across her wife’s face suggest a question mark. 

The title hints at a clinical examination, but Gribbon opens up a broader inquiry into how we perceive one another. Recognition takes time, unfolding as we linger over the painting’s ambiguities. 

Take a closer look at "Examinationscape" in "Jenna Gribbon: Entwined" at the Rose Art Museum. 

\_\_\_\_\_\_ 
Jenna Gribbon, "Examinationscape," 2021. Oil on Canvas. Tia Collection. Todd-White Art Photography. Courtesy of the artist, David Kordansky Gallery, and MASSIMODECARLO. © Jenna Gribbon.

[Favorites 286](https://www.instagram.com/p/DfaTspinS2p/) [Comments 0](https://www.instagram.com/p/DfaTspinS2p/)

10 days ago

Some paintings draw you across the gallery. Others pull you closer. 

In "Jenna Gribbon: Entwined," scale shapes the encounter. An enlarged face commands attention, while a smaller portrait invites you to lean in and linger over a gesture, an expression, or a brushstroke. Each holds its own power, shifting how we relate to the person pictured. 

Spend time with paintings large and small this weekend at the Rose Art Museum. There’s something about seeing them in person that a screen can’t quite capture. 

\_\_\_\_\_\_ 
Installation view, "Jenna Gribbon: Entwined," Rose Art Museum, Brandeis University, August 19, 2026–January 3, 2027. Julia Featheringill Photography. 

#jennagribbon #roseartmuseum #contemporaryart

[Favorites 113](https://www.instagram.com/p/DfW_nPJDrfi/) [Comments 5](https://www.instagram.com/p/DfW_nPJDrfi/)

11 days ago

Join artist @alisoncroneymoses for a talk about how woodworking and lived experience shape her sculptural practice. Moses will share how she uses techniques such as coopering and bent lamination to create curving wooden forms, and reflect on how her work explores pregnancy, childbirth, caregiving, belonging, and connection. 

📅 Friday, November 6, at 2:30 p.m. 
📍 Please note: The talk takes place at the Liberman-Miller Lecture Hall in the Women’s Studies Research Center, 515 South St., Waltham—not at the Rose Art Museum. 

Free and open to the public. Register through the link in our bio. 

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ 
Alison Croney Moses, photo by Jesika Theos.

[Favorites 280](https://www.instagram.com/p/DfUaBxFjIoj/) [Comments 4](https://www.instagram.com/p/DfUaBxFjIoj/)

12 days ago

Two galleries, one shared conversation. This Friday, November 6, at noon, explore how artists respond to displacement, cultural history, and the search for belonging on a Cross-Campus Tour at Brandeis. 

We’ll begin at the Kniznick Gallery with “They make a desolation and they call it peace,” where ten artists consider migration, resistance, and care through works shaped by personal and generational experiences of violence. Then, we’ll walk together to the Rose Art Museum to continue the conversation through “En/Lighten: Material and Metaphor” and “Yinka Shonibare: Sanctuary,” exploring light and architecture as expressions of hope, refuge, and possibility. 

Take a closer look, share your perspective, and discover connections across the exhibitions. 

Register through the link in our bio.

[Favorites 31](https://www.instagram.com/p/DfR1OxCAY4B/) [Comments 0](https://www.instagram.com/p/DfR1OxCAY4B/)

15 days ago

Devils, dark humor, political anxieties… it must be late October. 🎃 

In #FranciscoGoya’s "Subir y bajar (To Rise and To Fall)" (1799), a grinning devil hoists one figure into the air while others tumble below, creating a scene of instability, ambition, and sudden reversal. 

The print is plate 56 from Goya’s Los Caprichos, a series of 80 etchings published in 1799 that used fantasy, grotesque imagery, and biting satire to take aim at superstition, hypocrisy, social convention, and human folly. 

More than two centuries later, Goya’s strange world of ambition, uncertainty, and reversals of fortune still feels eerily familiar. 

#HappyHalloween from the Rose! 👻

## Dig Deeper

From Chinese art to the arts of the Islamic world, from Biblical manuscripts to Southeast Asian art, from the ancient Near East to the United States—our collections speak to the many meanings of Asia and its relationship to the rest of the world.

[Experience Our Collections](https://asia.si.edu/explore-art-culture/collections/search)

## Geography

How does place inform art? What role does place play in what is made, how it’s made, and who makes it? How does the art of one country or continent influence others?

Investigate the intersections of artworks from around the world through their unique stories and contexts.

## Presentation, Preservation, and Perspectives

We’re committed to placing masterworks of Asian art in dialogue with each other, with history, and with our American collection. We are committed to looking at the past critically, engaging with the present honestly, and envisioning the future inclusively.

[Our Vision & Values](https://asia.si.edu/about/mission-vision/)

Our vision is to transform the National Museum of Asian Art into a space where a wide range of visitors can come together to celebrate, learn about, and interact with Asian art and cultures, including their intersection with America. In our second century, we’re becoming a space to convene, learn, reflect, and forge connections through art.

Chase F. Robinson 
Director of the National Museum of Asian Art
